chapter: Radio color line, San Francisco and Columbia staff
title: Running and padlocking a San Francisco club
summary: In San Francisco Lee took over a club whose owner owed taxes, paid weekly toward them for ten weeks, then padlocked it after a dispute with a partner.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Yeah. I had still -- I had the little band I was telling you about, and I went up to San Francisco, and I was working in a club up there called the California Club, and right around the corner, Jack McVay had a band that he was working in a place -- I don't recall the name of it, but you know, that's where Vernon Alley -- you know, the bass player -- was from up there.

And they had a lot of music and a lot of places for music in San Francisco, but I stayed up there, maybe for a year, you know, off and on, and what happened -- this is where I first got my little thrown in to the place of business -- you know, we worked at this club, and the gentleman who owned the club, he didn't pay the taxes, you know, the franchise tax or whatever it is, and they came to put a lock on the place. Now, we were from Los Angeles, and nobody was paid or anything, and so I went downtown to see the people about it -- why, you know, why were they closing, all of our
instruments and everything was in there, and I told him we were from Los Angeles.

Well, the gentleman I was speaking to happened to be a Mason, you know, and I've been one all my life, practically, and so when I came back, he told me that he would let me run the club, if I paid them -- if I tried to pay the back taxes and I kept it up current.

Now I knew as much about running the club, or running any type of business, you know, that -- just nothing, you know, so I told him I would try it. And I actually tried it. And I did it for, like, 10 weeks -- but there was a partner involved with me, you know, and he was like held over from the other man that he had kicked out, and he blamed everything on the other man, but, somehow, these government people just said they left it up to me to see -- we were supposed to pay them like a thousand dollars a week on the back taxes he owed them, and you were supposed to keep it weekly.

And so I found out how to do it, and every week I would deposit their money; they told me how to deposit their money -- every week, and I did it for 10 weeks, and then all of a sudden, this guy wanted to pull some shennanigans, you know? So he and I had a bitter argument, you know, and so he was a big dude and he thought he was quite bad, so I told him, 'Well, okay, when you get ready to go to the club tonight, the club will have a padlock on it.'

And so, you know, he was laughing; he thought I was kidding; he didn't think I could do it. So I went downstairs and I told them that they should close the club because I wasn't gonna have anything todo with it any more, and you know, I kept my commitment and I had given my word and I thought they should close it.

So I went down and padlocked the club. And so we were on the next bus home, but that was really some kind of experience; that was the first time that I realized that I could really maybe take care of some type of business, you know? And you never know, as a musician, you know, because that's all you do all your life is to play music, and ...
